topics.title: Spatial vendor games, chess, and zero-sum games
quotes:
Answer: True
A simple proof by contradiction:   Let us assume this is a Nash.   If this is
a Nash, no one should have incentive to deviate. However, any of the vendors
at the end can do strictly better by moving towards the midpoint of the line.
Thus, it cannot be that the proposed outcome is a Nash Equilibrium

Proof by contradiction.   Let us assume that, with perfect information, the
outcome is unknown.   In that case, at least two of three end states must be
possible and occur with non-zero probability:   white wins, black wins, or the
game draws. We should be able to work backwards from each state to the start
of the game. There must, thus, be some point of departure in the order of play
that reaches each of the two or more potential final outcomes. The last player
who plays has strict preferences on which outcome they want (win¿draw¿loss).
Thus, the last player who decides which path the game goes down has a strict
preference and thus would not randomize. Therefore, the outcome of the game
must be certain.

Proof by counterexample: A zero sum game requires only that the payoffs
in each cell adds to zero.   Thus, trivially, we can have a game where all cells
are identical, let’s say they contain (0,0) for simplicity. In this case all strategy
pairs are Nash equilibria.

Answer:   We would expect the first player to always play Hawk and the
second dove.   We find this by backwards induction on the game tree.   If the
first player played Hawk, the second player would always prefer dove (0¿-1),
conversely, if the first player played Dove, the second player would prefer Hawk
(4¿2). The first player; thus, would prefer to play Hawk to get 4 instead of 0 in
the subgame perfect equilibrium.

This question is open ended, but one formulation of the answer is as follows:
The US took advantage of the Hawk-Dove structure of nuclear brinkmanship
to gain an advantage. By playing a more aggressive, threatening stance first, the
only truly viable strategy for the USSR was to back down or risk the destruction
of the world. In essence, by threatening escalation first, the USSR can respond
by escalating leading to nuclear war or backing down and losing their strategic
position in Cuba.

This game does not have a Nash equilibrium.   A Nash equilibrium in this
style of vendor game requires that they converge to a point where they split the
area or population exactly in half in every conceivable way to cut the shape. In
other words, we need a centrally symmetric point, where every line that cuts
the shape in half intersects. Such a point does not exist for a trapezoid. Thus,
a Nash equilibrium does not exist.   A player can deviate at any given point
towards one of the bisecting lines and do better, since not all bisecting lines
meet at one point.

topics.title: Commonsense and infinite Centipede equilibria
quotes:
Players seeing a long pattern of repetition may seek to minimize regret, and,
thus, choose some degree of early cooperation rather than accepting an outcome
of zero. More practically, a random individual when faced with this game may
not think so pessimistically as to assume cooperation will immediately break
down even if it is rational. In such a case, believing there is a chance for some
length of cooperation may lead to a different outcome if the belief is mutual.

Let us assume that both players choosing Pass every time is not a Nash
Equilibrium. Thus, one of the players must take at some period. However, this
player knows that if they Pass on this period and take the next time they have
a turn will yield strictly more for them.   Thus, they would delay taking.   As
the game is infinite, this logic does not break down due to the end of the game;
thus, always Passing is a Nash Equilibrium.

If both players always play Keep, no one player benefit from deviating. Any
deviation past the first period does not change payoffs, since the first player
already took. However, on the first turn, choosing to Pas will yield strictly less,
as player two will then immediately take.   Thus, both players choosing Keep
every time is likewise a Nash Equilibrium.
